EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the afternoon of March 7th, a line of showers and thunderstorms tracked into the Chautauqua County from Pennsylvania. As the storms tracked northeast, they became severe causing a few reports of damage in Chautauqua and then Cattaraugus counties. The storms were within the warm sector of a surface low located near Lake Huron, developing and strengthening along a pre-frontal trough that was crossing the region. Timing with afternoon heating and a strong low level jet that increased shear over the area coincided with the trough passage to cause a cluster of thunderstorms to become severe.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Two utility poles and three lines downed. 180 Upper Road.

A large area of low pressure tracking from the mid-Mississippi Valley and across the Central Great Lakes caused strong winds for portions of the area. As the surface low approached the region it strengthened, resulting in increased pressure gradient over the region. Coupled with a strong low level jet and a southeasterly flow within warm air advection, downslope winds in Chautauqua and Southern Erie county became very strong. Wind gusts of 74 and 72 MPH were recorded with the downslope conditions for this event.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: At the Fredonia NYS Mesonet. Also 63 knots at the Dunkirk Airport.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong low pressure system brought a period of strong winds, along with rain, to eastern New York on March 16-17, 2026. Winds started in the southerly direction before switching to the west behind the cold front. Widespread wind gusts of 40 to 50 mph were observed with some localized gusts approaching 60 mph. These winds along with the softer ground due to rain led to numerous reports of downed trees and wires. Approximately 48,000 customers lost power across eastern New York.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An estimated 2100 people were without power throughout Albany County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: After a very cold winter, a significant amount of ice, with substantial depth, developed on main-stem rivers across eastern New York. Periodic multi-day stretches of late-season, above-normal temperatures subsequently led to considerable ice melt over a short amount of time. This ultimately led to flooding in Schenectady and Saratoga Counties in early March after an ice jam broke loose on the Mohawk River. NWS Albany was made aware of the flooding and its requisite impacts from communication with both local news outlets and emergency managers in the area. As a direct result of the ice jam flooding, the SUNY Schenectady campus was closed on March 9th with all classes on campus cancelled due to associated parking lots and roadways inundated with low amounts of standing water. Additionally, NWS Albany was made aware that Rosendale Road between Mohawk Road and Niskayuna Road was closed due to flooding from this same ice jam. However, local emergency managers in the area stated that this flooding was more minor compared to the flooding in Saratoga County. Here, the town of Halfmoon sustained more significant impacts with the closure of Riverview Road near Boyack Road. In a recording of a local news report, water from a small stream stemming off the Mohawk River was overrunning a low point in the road to a fairly significant extent. The water was also moving at the time of the broadcast and the reporter noted that it had begun to recede compared to what it had been. Luckily, it only took about 24 hours or so for the flooding to recede from all areas, allowing the aforementioned roadways and the SUNY Schenectady Campus to promptly re-open by the following morning.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: NWS Albany Meteorologists contacted the Schenectady County Warning Point to seek more information about flooding from an ice jam that had been reported on by a local news team. The warning point relayed that Rosendale Road was closed between Mohawk Road and Niskayuna Road due to the same ice jam.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The combination of persistent rounds of moderate to heavy rainfall; above-normal temperatures; and subsequent snowmelt led to several days worth of significant flooding along the West Canada Creek in Herkimer County.||The West Canada Creek USGS river gauge at Hinckley Reservoir reported minor flooding beginning around 9:45 PM EDT on March 31. The gauge then rose to moderate flood stage around 2:00 AM EDT on April 1. The creek crested just below major flood stage at 1229.82 feet around 4:30 PM EDT on April 1 before slowly receding over the next several days.| |The West Canada Creek USGS river gauge at Kast Bridge reported minor flooding beginning at 9:15 PM EDT on March 31st. The gauge reached then reached moderate flood stage by 1:45 AM EDT on April 1st. By 4:45 PM EDT on April 1, the gauge reached major flood stage where it later crested at 8.21 feet during the late evening hours on April 1st. Thereafter, gradual receding of flood waters saw the gauge readings drop below flood stage on April 3rd at 6:15 PM EDT. ||Along the entire path of the West Canada Creek, various towns and villages were affected by this flooding with areal images and videos showing water encroaching on river-adjacent homes, roadways, and local businesses including in Poland, Newport and Middleville. In Newport, two homes were evacuated and had power supply cut off due to flood waters inundating the property. State Route 28 and other surrounding roads were closed for several days also due to inundation by flood waters and the American Red Cross set up a relief shelter at the Kuyahoora Community Hall in order to provide those impacted with necessary supplies. Additionally, Kast Bridge itself was closed due to dangerously high water levels threatening to inundate it.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The combination of heavy rain and snow melt led to the West Canada Creek to overflow its banks from Hinckley Reservoir down to Kast Bridge and slightly farther downstream. Local news stations shared pictures and videos of flooding occurring in spots along the entire path of the creek from Poland to Newport and Middleville with water encroaching on river-adjacent homes, roadways, and local businesses.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On March 31st, severe thunderstorms moved across Lake Erie and into portions of southwestern New York as a potent shortwave trough crossed the area with a stationary front draped across the south shore of Lake Ontario and lake breeze boundaries found across the area. Shear values of 40+ knots and instability values of around 1,000 J/kg at the time the trough crossed the area combined for a favorable setup for severe thunderstorms. EVENT_NARRATIVE: The National Weather Service in Buffalo investigated storm-related |damage from a rotating thunderstorm that affected the area southeast |of Machias in Cattaraugus County on March 31st. The National Weather |Service storm survey team investigated the damage in the area and confirmed damage consistent with an EF-1 tornado with estimated peak winds of 107 mph. The tornado had a path length of 1.4 miles, and a maximum width of 150 yards.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A pair of cold fronts brought abnormally cold temperatures on March 17th and 18th. The cool temperatures over the warmer lake waters of both Lake Erie and Lake Ontario setup a lake response off of the lakes, but conditions over and lee of Lake Ontario were more favorable. Lake Effect snow developed on the morning of March 17th northeast of the lakes. By the mid morning, the lake band off of Lake Ontario dropped south, focusing on Oswego County for the remainder of the day and into the early morning of the 18th. Oswego County received the most snow as the lake band oscillated back and forth north to south. ||Notable snowfall amounts include: 13.4 inches in Fulton, 10.0 inches in Altmar and 9.2 inches in Palermo.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: After a very cold winter, a significant amount of ice, with substantial depth, developed on main-stem rivers across eastern New York. Periodic multi-day stretches of late-season, above-normal temperatures subsequently led to considerable ice melt over a short amount of time. This ultimately led to flooding in Schenectady and Saratoga Counties in early March after an ice jam broke loose on the Mohawk River. NWS Albany was made aware of the flooding and its requisite impacts from communication with both local news outlets and emergency managers in the area. As a direct result of the ice jam flooding, the SUNY Schenectady campus was closed on March 9th with all classes on campus cancelled due to associated parking lots and roadways inundated with low amounts of standing water. Additionally, NWS Albany was made aware that Rosendale Road between Mohawk Road and Niskayuna Road was closed due to flooding from this same ice jam. However, local emergency managers in the area stated that this flooding was more minor compared to the flooding in Saratoga County. Here, the town of Halfmoon sustained more significant impacts with the closure of Riverview Road near Boyack Road. In a recording of a local news report, water from a small stream stemming off the Mohawk River was overrunning a low point in the road to a fairly significant extent. The water was also moving at the time of the broadcast and the reporter noted that it had begun to recede compared to what it had been. Luckily, it only took about 24 hours or so for the flooding to recede from all areas, allowing the aforementioned roadways and the SUNY Schenectady Campus to promptly re-open by the following morning.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A local news station reporter was seen reporting from Riverview Road in the town of Halfmoon in Saratoga County on the evening of March 9th. In their report, they stated that Riverview Road was closed near Boyack Road in Halfmoon. Here, water from a small stream stemming off the Mohawk River was overrunning a low point in the road, causing the closure. According to the report, water was beginning to recede just before 7 PM when it had, just an hour prior, been rather high.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A highly anticipated, highly impactful Nor'easter struck eastern New York on the evening of Sunday, February 22 through the afternoon of Monday, February 23, 2026. Tracking along the East Coast and rapidly intensifying as it approached the 40 latitude/70 longitude benchmark, this system quickly gained national attention not only for its projected widespread blizzard conditions across many high profile, highly populated areas, but for the complexity of its forecast.||Confidence increased sufficiently for forecasters at National Weather Service Albany to upgrade prior issued Winter Storm Warnings to a Blizzard Warnings in Dutchess and Ulster Counties mere hours prior to snowfall onset. Once snow began, it didn't take long for rates to become moderate to heavy, particularly across Dutchess and eastern Ulster Counties, rapidly dropping visibility late in the evening of Sunday, February 22nd. As the core of the still strengthening storm drew closer, winds became gusty and reduced visibility further. The combination of heavy snowfall rates and frequent wind gusts between 25 to 40 mph made for on and off blizzard conditions, with visibilities falling below one quarter of a mile, from around 3 AM through nearly 2 PM Monday, February 23, 2026 across Dutchess and eastern Ulster Counties. Snow finally began to gradually slow after 2 PM Monday, February 23, 2026 and eventually tapered off after 4 PM. The resulting snowfall totals across Dutchess and eastern Ulster Counties ranged from 7 to 18 inches.||As previously mentioned, this was a very complicated forecast. Model guidance in the days leading up to the event was highly variable in their depictions of the track and strength of the system. Ultimately, the track of the storm remained farther south and east than what was anticipated, leading to a fairly steep southeast to northwest gradient in snowfall totals. However, by the following night, widespread dangerously cold temperatures overtook the region with minimum air temperatures ranging from -22 to 6 degrees Fahrenheit and minimum feels-like temperatures spanning -36 to -2 degrees Fahrenheit. A brief respite came on January 30th when extensive cloud cover maintained sufficient insulation to limit temperature falls, but by the next night, February 1, minimum feels-like temperatures once again fell to -34 to -5 degrees Fahrenheit.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Minimum low temperature of -5 degrees Fahrenheit recorded with a minimum wind chill of -28 degrees Fahrenheit.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Low pressure in the gulf states moved northeast and intensified along and off the Mid Atlantic coast with the consolidated of mid level energy resulting in a major Nor'easter which brought blizzard and near blizzard conditions to Southeastern New York. The storm became vertically stacked and it slowly pulled away to the east and brought a heavy to major snowfall across Southeastern New York with blizzard conditions across Southern Westchester, New York City, and Long Island.  Winter storm and near blizzard conditions were reported across the remainder of Southeastern New York. A major snowfall occurred region wide, with portions of the region receiving historic snowfall totals.||A college student died from carbon monoxide poisoning while charging his cell phone during the blizzard. Also, there were 5 snow shoveling-related deaths on Long Island after the blizzard.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Frequent wind gusts of over 50 mph with JFK ASOS reporting a 62 mph gust at 5:17 am, a 64 mph gust at Kew Garden Hills NYS mesonet at 3:20 am, and a 50 mph gust reported at 2:16 am at the Breezy Point mesonet station, and a 57 mph gust reported at Brooklyn College NYSM station at 5:10 am; along with frequent visibilities of a quarter mile or less were reported at the JFK ASOS. Snowfall amounts reported across the zone ranged just on either side of 20 inches across the zone via public reports, trained spotters, and the official NWS observation at JFK airport.

However, by the following night, widespread dangerously cold temperatures overtook the region with minimum air temperatures ranging from -22 to 6 degrees Fahrenheit and minimum feels-like temperatures spanning -36 to -2 degrees Fahrenheit. A brief respite came on January 30th when extensive cloud cover maintained sufficient insulation to limit temperature falls, but by the next night, February 1, minimum feels-like temperatures once again fell to -34 to -5 degrees Fahrenheit.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Minimum wind chill of -19 degrees Fahrenheit recorded.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A potent cold front ushered a bitterly cold airmass into eastern New York on January 23-24, 2026. The combination of bitterly cold air temperatures (minimum temperatures ranging from -34 to 5 degrees Fahrenheit) and gusty winds (ranging from 25 to nearly 50 mph) made for dangerously cold wind chills or feels-like temperatures. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the afternoon of February 3rd, a snow squall developed along a cold front crossing the region. As the snow squall crossed the area, visibilities dropped to quarter of a mile or less at times. Snow squall warnings were issued for many areas near/along the I90 corridor.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snow squall.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the evening of February 18th, a thunderstorm developed over Lake Erie and tracked southeast onshore across southern Erie County. As the thunderstorm tracked onshore it strengthened and briefly became severe. The combination of favorable mid-level lapse rates, low freezing levels and shear allowed the storm to strengthen enough to produce one inch hail in Angola. After producing the hail, the storm quickly weakened as it continued to track across Erie County.

A trough feature developed and extended west from the intensifying offshore low that enhanced snowfall across far eastern portions of the county warning area, specifically the eastern end of Long Island and impacting the twin forks with heavy snow and wind.

The public also reported 4.5 inches in Sag Harbor. Amounts dropped off once west of the southern fork with a general 2 to 5 inches reported across the western portion of the zone. The heavier snowfall and wind impacted mainly the south fork of the island.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An arctic cold front blasted across northern NY during the early morning hours of February 7th sending temperatures plummeting near and below zero on brisk northwest winds of 10 to 20 mph with higher gusts creating dangerous windchill temperatures of 20 to 35 below zero for the daylight hours of February 7th. ||Although winds diminished somewhat on the night of the 7th, sub-zero temperatures still accounted for 25 to 40 below wind chills through midday on February 8th with daytime wind chills still 15 to 25 below zero.||Arctic high pressure crested across the region on the night of February 8th into the morning hours of February 9th. This allowed temperatures to radiate down to 10 to 25 below zero across northern NY.||This was the 3rd such cold spell within the past month that attributed to the Ice Over of Lake Champlain on February 13th, the first time since 2018.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Daytime temperatures falling to the single digits above zero on Saturday (2/7) combined with northwest winds of 10 to 20 mph with higher gusts created wind chills of 10 to 20 below zero during the daylight hours. ||Saturday night (2/7) - Sunday morning (2/8)...although winds diminished to 5 to 10 mph and gusty at times, actual air temperatures fell to 5 to 10 below zero creating dangerous wind chills of 20 to 30 below zero. During Sunday (2/8) temperatures were 0 to 10 degrees above zero but a persistent wind around 10 mph created wind chills up to 10 below zero. High pressure crested across the region during the overnight into the early morning hours of February 9th, allowing temperatures to fall to near 10 below zero.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong low pressure moved into the Great Lakes on March 16th and into northern Quebec Canada by the morning of March 17th. This storm brought blizzard conditions across the MN,WI and the western Great Lakes while the sharp cold front brought severe weather outbreaks from TX/OK eastward to the Atlantic coast.||Strong southerly winds, ahead of the low pressure, during the early morning hours of March 16th brought 50 to 70 mph wind gusts across northern NY that resulted in several reports of tree limbs or trees in utility lines and several thousand power outages across northern NY. A sharp cold front associated with the strong low pressure moved across northern NY just prior to midnight on the 16-17th with a short duration of 40-50+ mph wind gusts and some additional damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several wind gusts in excess of 40-45 mph from the south of March 16th and then from the west during the early morning hours of March 17th after the passage of a sharp cold front.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Low pressure in the gulf states moved northeast and intensified along and off the Mid Atlantic coast with the consolidated of mid level energy resulting in a major Nor'easter which brought blizzard and near blizzard conditions to Southeastern New York. The storm became vertically stacked and it slowly pulled away to the east and brought a heavy to major snowfall across Southeastern New York with blizzard conditions across Southern Westchester, New York City, and Long Island.  Winter storm and near blizzard conditions were reported across the remainder of Southeastern New York. A major snowfall occurred region wide, with portions of the region receiving historic snowfall totals.||A college student died from carbon monoxide poisoning while charging his cell phone during the blizzard. Also, there were 5 snow shoveling-related deaths on Long Island after the blizzard.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Frequent wind gusts of over 40 mph with LGA ASOS reporting a 52 mph gust at 6:04 am, and a 64 mph gust at Kew Garden Hills NYS mesonet at 3:20 am; along with frequent visibilities of a quarter mile or less were reported at the LGA ASOS. Snowfall amounts reported across the zone ranged from mainly 18 to 23 inches across the zone via public reports, trained spotters, and the official NWS observation at LGA airport.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A persistent polar airmass created a prolonged period of frigid conditions across eastern New York for the final days of January into the very beginning of February. Bitter cold air temperatures combined with periods of gusty winds and fresh, deep snowpack made for several days worth of dangerously cold conditions. ||The cold outbreak began early on January 29th where the most dangerously cold minimum wind chill values, or feels-like temperatures, were noted across the higher terrain areas of the Southern Adirondacks, Eastern Catskills, Mohawk Valley, and Taconics. A brief respite came on January 30th when extensive cloud cover maintained sufficient insulation to limit temperature falls, but by the next night, February 1, minimum feels-like temperatures once again fell to -34 to -5 degrees Fahrenheit.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Minimum wind chill of -23 degrees Fahrenheit recorded.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A blockbuster winter storm that impacted millions across the lower 48, bringing a combination of ice; sleet; snow; rain; and strong winds, brought widespread heavy snowfall accumulations to all of eastern New York from January 25-26th, 2026. ||An arctic blast made for dangerously cold conditions across eastern New York from January 23-24, creating a requisite cold airmass that supported snow as the primary precipitation type with this storm. The connection of the northern and southern stream flow regimes then steered a potent, Gulf-originating low pressure system to the northeast. Strong to anomalous low- to mid-level dynamics drove impressive moisture transport from the Gulf and western Atlantic in and across the region the morning of the impending storm, Sunday January 25th. Snow began Sunday morning, initially with a large dendritic growth zone courtesy of persistent arctic air being filtered into the region from northerly flow about a nearby surface high to the northeast. However, as the storm tracked closer, its associated warm nose modified the thermal profile and shrunk and lifted the dendritic growth zone into the mid and upper levels of the atmosphere by the afternoon. Snowfall rates that initially looked to reach up to 2-4 per hour within laterally translating snow bands therefore became limited to 1-2 per hour courtesy of the disconnect between the best low-level forcing and the dendritic growth zone. Still, a widespread 10-20 of snow fell across the region between Sunday, January 25th and Monday, January 26th. ||The expansive impacts that this storm had on New York State as a whole led Governor Kathy Hochul to declare a widespread State of Emergency which encompassed all of our portion of eastern New York. NWS Albany received reports of numerous school and road closures in addition to traffic accidents across eastern New York. ||Key Impacts: state of emergency declarations, road closures, school closures, travel restrictions, traffic accidents.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Zone average snowfall of 15.7 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A persistent polar airmass created a prolonged period of frigid conditions across eastern New York for the final days of January into the very beginning of February. Bitter cold air temperatures combined with periods of gusty winds and fresh, deep snowpack made for several days worth of dangerously cold conditions. ||The cold outbreak began early on January 29th where the most dangerously cold minimum wind chill values, or feels-like temperatures, were noted across the higher terrain areas of the Southern Adirondacks, Eastern Catskills, Mohawk Valley, and Taconics. However, by the following night, widespread dangerously cold temperatures overtook the region with minimum air temperatures ranging from -22 to 6 degrees Fahrenheit and minimum feels-like temperatures spanning -36 to -2 degrees Fahrenheit. A brief respite came on January 30th when extensive cloud cover maintained sufficient insulation to limit temperature falls, but by the next night, February 1, minimum feels-like temperatures once again fell to -34 to -5 degrees Fahrenheit.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Minimum low temperature of -3 degrees Fahrenheit recorded with a minimum wind chill of -21 degrees Fahrenheit.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Low pressure in the gulf states moved northeast and intensified along and off the Mid Atlantic coast with the consolidated of mid level energy resulting in a major Nor'easter which brought blizzard and near blizzard conditions to Southeastern New York. The storm became vertically stacked and it slowly pulled away to the east and brought a heavy to major snowfall across Southeastern New York with blizzard conditions across Southern Westchester, New York City, and Long Island.  Winter storm and near blizzard conditions were reported across the remainder of Southeastern New York. A major snowfall occurred region wide, with portions of the region receiving historic snowfall totals.||A college student died from carbon monoxide poisoning while charging his cell phone during the blizzard. Also, there were 5 snow shoveling-related deaths on Long Island after the blizzard.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Most reports across the county came in at 12 to 15 inches with near blizzard conditions reported across much of Rockland County, with the higher amounts generally across southeastern portions of the county. Amateur radio observations of 15.9 inches at New City, and 12.0 inches in Thiells was reported. Cocorahs observers reported 15.9 inches at 1.7 SSW Spring Valley; and 10.3 inches in Stony Point before accumulations ended.
